At the edge of the yard Burgundy glanced back and saw Ran watching him go, and knew he had not been fooled, and that Ran had decided not to ask. Not to know.
They climbed back through the freeze as the sun was finishing its feeble rise for the day, the sky turning a grey blue, and large flakes of slow snow wandered their way to the ground.

The two boys passed the bundle of parts between them when their arms got cold, and Tuck talked the whole way, low at first and then back to his big self, going on about a cook who had wept over a sauce he botched, and about the critter who snuck into the cold storage and they found it frozen solid, and Burgundy laughed twice, out loud, which he never did inside the walls, because inside the walls there was no one to laugh with.

Halfway up Tuck stopped to breathe and looked back down at all of it, the stacked and lit-up dark, the gold fog of the market floor, a vein of orange among the blue, and ten thousand stovepipes going up into the cobalt sky.
"Best place on the planet," Tuck said, "and they built the palace so you'd never get to even look at it." He grinned. "Idiots."
Burgundy looked at it too, breathing hard from the climb. He had come down here thinking the machine in the basement was his, a thing he had made because he was made different. Special.

But then he had watched a man run a pump and a fire off one motor. He had watched a boy his own age wind a perfect coil with a mill crank. Nobody on that slope lacked the mind to build what he built. They lacked the parts. Parts, and the time to waste.
And in that moment he so deeply wanted to give them all of it. He did not know yet what that meant, and he did not chase it. He just carried it up the hill with him with his bundle of parts.

chapters.title: chapter 9 Nicholas
paragraphs: That was the boy he had been.
They snuck out five more times that year, and the sixth time the security minister's people were waiting at the low gate.
Soon he was in the office of his furious father

*He was sixteen*, he seethed. *Nearly a man*, and there would be *no more of the cook's boy. Kings did not keep friends in the kitchens*. It was time he learned the difference between the people he ruled and the people he kept.
So that was the end of it. Not a falling out. He and Tuck were just pulled back to opposite ends of the same hall, by the same force that did it the first time.
Tuck was in the kitchens still. They passed sometimes, two minutes at a time, and neither of them ever talked about their little flash of adventure and friendship when they were thirteen.

And now he was seventeen years old, and sitting at a long dark oiled table in his mother's secret library, wondering what he would do in the white room behind the yellow book. And how he would make good on the other side of the bargain, the promise to become the *Prince your father expects you to be.*

From that day on he lived two lives. Protocol ruled one. Sunlight streaming through a thousand panes of glass and stone. An embroidered coat, as he performed his expected role. The other took place after dusk, behind a nondescript yellow book high up on a shelf.

Burgundy threw himself into being the perfect prince, but the work took a toll. He felt it grind him down. A dull ache behind his eyes always after a day of it. It was the quiet hours working in the secret bright white room, surrounded by possibilities, that renewed him.
The months went on and neither life knew about the other, and Burgundy carried an increasing fear that his father was on to him.

But the more time passed, the more he realized Mira was right. His father seemed to believe nothing was amiss. That the lecture had worked. The days he spent in the light of the colorful window, by his father's side, he realized that the King saw the son he expected to see, the boy finally bent into shape, and he did not look further.
He had a growing curiosity about Nicholas, The tribute. The arrangement the planet was in. How did it work?

He stayed late one after council. The council chamber emptied slowly, Burgundy waited until it was nearly clear and then went to the steward at the side door, an older man he had seen every day of his life and could not have named.
"The old ledgers," Burgundy said. "The tribute accounts. Where are they kept."
"With the master of records, sir."
"And where is he."
"I could not say, sir." The steward looked at a point just past Burgundy's shoulder, the way they all did. "Shall I send word that the prince asked?"
Which meant his father would hear of it by evening. Burgundy heard the protective trap in the courtesy and stepped back from it.
"No," he said. "It's nothing. I was just curious."

"Very good, sir," the steward said, and held the door, and did not watch him go, and Burgundy went out into the corridor thinking that his mother had used that same word, curious, and made it sound like the most dangerous thing a person could be.
With time he was surprised now much he learned just sitting in council for hours a day listening. And after a few months he started to get the full picture on the Tribute.
Nicholas provided security. That was the word the ministers used, *security*, always without irony, and it took Burgundy three months of listening to understand everything the word contained.

Dross sat in a remote, dangerous part of a remote system, months of hard travel from the lanes of the Core World Alliance. The Alliance's markets were distant; its protection was theoretical. A planet full of minerals with no fleet of its own was like a warehouse of valuables with the doors unlocked. Nicholas kept the doors locked.

No one on Dross had ever met Nicholas. Not the King. Not the King's father, or his father. Four generations of the royal line had ruled this planet fearing Nicholas's name and not one of them had heard his voice or seen his face or received so much as a single word.
Nicholas's ships patrolled the approaches. But Nicholas's name, more than his ships, kept the raiders of six systems from descending onto Dross to pillage or conquer.

In exchange, Nicholas took unrefined ore. Around 70% of what they produced. The royalty of Dross had resented the bargain for four generations and yet for four generations they had complied, because it worked, and because nothing else would.
Every resource-rich planet in the region lived under some version of this arrangement. It was not an alliance. It was extortion with a schedule. The ministers did not call it that.
Burgundy learned to come early to council

The ministers gathered before the King arrived, in the grey hour, before the sun illuminated the big window's panes. They warmed up over stimulating root tea, bitter and faintly numbing. Sweet bread, torn and passed. Loose talk, before they put their public faces on.
He said little.
This morning they were discussing  collection, which was five days out, the tally sheet spread down the main table. Burgundy set down his cup. "What happens if we come up short?"
The table looked at him. It was the first meaningful question he'd ever asked to these people.
The oldest man in the room answers. Vharush was the minister of mining. He a face like a TK,  one eye gone milk-pale from a rockburst forty years down.

He glanced once at the closed doors before he spoke. "It's happened. only once in recent memory, before your time. Eastern works, a governor came up short on corvite one month, and didn't know it." He tore his bread. took a sip of tea "Bad count. Books said he was fine. Eight percent short and nobody caught it."
"So what happened?" Burgundy said.

"The ship came, took the load, left, same as any month. Three days on, another ship came back. Didn't collect. Came down over the governor's own house, hundred meters up, and stopped." Vharush turned the bread in his fingers. "Eleven days. this huge ship, big as a district, hanging over his roof, throwing his compound into shadow half of every day. Took nothing. Dropped nothing. Sent no word. Just hung there."
The room had gone quiet.
"By then they'd torn the books and weight logs apart and found the eight percent discrepancy and had to get to work.

Whole shafts on round-the-clock shifts. By the twelfth day the governor had the missing stuff and shipped it to the capital, flew along side the rigs as they drove to deliver it himself. The ships followed,  Ship took it that night off the cargo field and was gone by morning. Never a word, start to finish."

"There," the trade minister said, reaching for the tallies. "That is why the count has to be right the first time. That is why the sharpest men on Dross sit in the Custom House and nowhere else. We do not miss eight percent."
Burgundy was confused about something, "But how did he know it was that one governor who had fallen short. Aren't all the minerals pooled together for the collection"

"That's the part I never followed." said a young minister who had been looking at his cup, rotating it in his hand.  Every district pools into the one house before it ships.  There's no line in any book that says which region came up short. So how did Nicholas know whose house to sit over?"
A pause. One or two of them frowned at the question, thinking
"Bad count's a bad count," Vharush said, and reached for the bread. "Point is you don't hand him one."

Burgundy's mouth was. numb, his mind sharpening as the tea took effect. And in the silence and followed the story, he was taking in another lesson, not one about book keeping. The young minister had asked the only question that mattered, *how did he know,* and Vharush had answered with a proverb about accounting.

These were the smartest men on the planet. ANd every ounce of their effort went into one thing: *get the number right, get it delivered, do not come up short. *That was the whole of their genius now. Not *why* they paid, or *whether* they could stop, or *what* it meant that a faceless man could find one guilty roof in a hundred districts. Those questions had been trained out of them, or out of their fathers.
The sun peered over the horizon and shot light through the vast window, shooting a million threads of lights into the vast hall. The King entered through the double doors, walking briskly.
"Good morning Gentlemen." he said in the cheer he wore in the last days before a collection. "Let's get to finalizing the tally."

chapters.title: chapter 10 TKK
paragraphs: The nights belonged to the white room.
He found his own ways up. That was the first project. His mother's route through the broom-closet stair was hers; using it risked pattern, and pattern risked notice.

The palace's roots were deeper than its towers. Old dungeon galleries, drainage vaults, dead corridors sealed and forgotten by men who had died before his grandfather was born. And through his exploration he discovered that Mira's wing had been built onto a disused arm of one of these subterranean complexes, its foundations grafted into the old cells.
Over the first month he mapped three separate routes from the basement to his mother's wing, each surfacing through a different forgotten door.
In the white room, for the first few months, he read. And only read.
He discovered that there was an entire universe of knowledge from the core worlds. The knowledge came on discs. And the discs, he came to understand, were the shape of the whole civilization.

There was no living connection between the stars. That was the fact underneath everything, the fact the Core World Alliance's own maps politely minimized: information could be beamed between worlds, but a signal was months crossing what a ship crossed in weeks, decayed and stuttering by the time it arrived. So knowledge moved the way freight moved: in batches, on hulls. The great relay stations of the core worlds gathered transmissions the way harbors gather cargo, wrote them onto discs, and the discs rode out along the trade lanes toward the periphery. A disc was a slab of pressed crystal the size of Burgundy's palm, dense with more text than the palace's three libraries combined, and by the time one reached Dross the research on it was a year old at minimum, often three. It did not matter. On Dross, three years behind the core was still fifty years ahead of anything else on the planet.

Mira's cousin brought the discs in with the cargo runs. They would come in a small wooden box with divider slits, packed with wool and sawdust. In those first few months, Burgundy began to crave these discs. He would slip his mother a written list, folded into the book she was reading at breakfast, and two or three weeks later a crate would arrive in the white room with the discs pressed between wool packing, labeled in a language he had begun teaching himself. He could slip a disc into his terminal and start reading: journals of the core-world academies, engineering symposium collections, survey papers that mapped whole fields in a single sitting, patent filings by the thousand, each one a blueprint of somebody's solved problem, and the discipline he hunted for across all of them, the research on teaching code to drive a mechanical body.
He devoured all of it. He had no desire to build anything until he had absorbed what the core worlds had discovered in their academies, generations of advanced knowledge.
Then the reading tipped over into his hands.

It came, the way most of it would come, off a disc. One night, working late on a symposium collection three years stale, he read a short paper on how a machine could be taught to close a hand around an object it could not see: not by measuring the object first and computing a grip, but by squeezing, slowly, while a gauge in each finger reported the strain, and stopping the instant the numbers said the hold was firm, and logging where firm had been so the next reach started closer to it. He read it twice. Then he got up from the terminal and went to the bench.

He had a hand already, of a kind, built in the first restless weeks when his fingers got tired of watching his eyes do all the work. Three jointed fingers off a scrapped press linkage, worked by a single salvaged servo through a loop of cable, wired to a board he had pulled out of a dead mine-elevator controller. It could open and it could close. That was the whole of what it could do. It closed the same on everything, and it had ground a clay cup to grit on one setting and on the same setting failed to lift a folded rag. He had set it aside as a toy that lied about being useful.

Now he went and got it. He soldered a strain gauge into each fingertip, the crude kind, off a scrapped shop scale, and he wrote the loop the paper described. Squeeze. Read the gauge. Stop where the number says the grip is true, and not one degree past it. Log the number. Start the next grip closer to it. He fed it the folded rag first. The hand closed, and felt, and held.
He gave it the clay cup.
The fingers came in until the cup pushed back, and then they stopped, and the cup stood whole in the metal hand.

It was the first time the hand had chosen. He had not told it the cup was fragile. It had found that out for itself, in the half second of closing, and it had stopped, and it would remember. He sat with it a long while, turning the cup out of the fingers and setting it back and watching the grip come in a little truer each pass, and somewhere in that hour the last of his patience for only reading burned off.

After that the two appetites ran together. He read to build, and he built to know what to read next. Every few weeks a crate came up from the cargo field in wool and sawdust, a dozen more of somebody's solved problems pressed into crystal, and he carried them down through the dark and fed them to the machine one paper at a time. Night by night the hand closed truer. Held longer. Learned the weight of one more thing without being told.

Then the hand outgrew the bench. It could hold anything he set in front of it and then it sat, waiting to be handed the next thing, and he was tired of being the thing that carried the work to it. He bolted the arm to a flat sled, put a single fat wheel under it off a scrapped serving cart, geared it low, and wrote it a crude sense of its own leading edge so it would not run itself off the table into the dark. The first night it moved, it crossed the bench, found the folded rag by touch, and stopped hard against a chock he had clamped down in case it did not stop at all. He took the chock away. The next night it stopped on its own.

chapters.title: chapter 11 The Custom House
paragraphs: By day he was the prince his father expected, and his father, believing the boy had finally come round, had begun to teach him in earnest. He had taken to it lately with a kind of appetite. Any hour he had his son beside him and a quiet minute to fill, he filled it with the craft, the real accounting of the thing, the parts of ruling he said no one would teach Burgundy honestly but him. Which was how Burgundy came to be crossing the square on a white morning, three steps behind the King, toward the Custom House at the head of it.

The square he knew. The founder's statue stood at the center of it, his grandfather cast in dark metal, one hand raised in a gesture the sculptor had meant for blessing and the freeze had streaked with rust, so that the old king appeared to be lifting a hand that had begun to bleed. Past the statue the low city fell away in its terraces of grey stone and rust roofing, smoke standing straight up off ten thousand stovepipes in the still cold. The Custom House was grey stone like everything the crown built, and its doors opened onto the statue's back.

Inside it was warm. Burgundy had lost the ability to walk into a warm room without doing the sum: whose coal, cut by whom, hauled how far, to keep the trade ministry at a temperature where the ink would not thicken in the wells.

The trade minister was waiting for them at a long table, a narrow man with ink worked so deep into the creases of his knuckles it would not wash out, and he had laid the ministry open for the prince the way another man might lay out a feast. Ledgers stood in ranks down the middle of the table. Along the wall, ore samples sat in glass cases, graded and labeled, a museum of everything the planet gave up. The minister loved his ledgers. It came off him the moment he began to speak, an unhurried pride, and Burgundy understood within a minute that he was about to be taught more about his own planet than seventeen years of living on it had managed.
"How many," Burgundy asked him. "How many minerals do we sell that are worth the shipping."

"Eleven," the minister said, pleased to be asked. "Eleven that pay. Iron in bulk out of the north, where the seams run shallow and wide, a boy could dig the north. Copper and tin from the eastern hills. The rest come up out of the deep shafts in the south, the ones that take men." He said take men the way he might have said take water, a line entered and carried forward. He moved down the cases as he spoke and let his ink-dark hand rest a moment on each. "Blue-black corvite, which goes off-world raw and comes back inside every processor in the galaxy. Threnite, which holds a charge. And a little osmarine, the stuff that weighs less than nothing and holds the lanes open between the stars."
He stopped at a case near the end and opened it and lifted out a small sealed ingot and set it in Burgundy's hand without ceremony.
It was heavier than it looked. Refined corvite, dense and cold and blue-black, a bar he could have closed his fist around, and it dragged at his wrist like a stone twice its size.

"That," the minister said, "graded fine and sealed, one crate of it, is worth more than a year of everything the northern fields pull out of the ground. More than all that iron. A crate you could carry on your shoulder against a year of the north's whole sweat."

Burgundy turned the ingot over. He thought about the number the way he thought about a torque figure, testing whether it could be true, and decided it could. Then he asked the question that was already sitting in him, because it was the only question an engineer could ask, holding a thing that valuable.
"Then why do we send it raw."
The minister's pleasure faltered for the first time. He glanced, quickly, at the King.

"We sell the ore," the King said. He had not spoken since they came in. He was standing at the window with his back to them, looking out at the statue of his father from behind, and he spoke without turning around. "It goes off my ground raw and comes back at four times the price with somebody else's mark on it. I made my peace with that a long time ago. You will too."
"Why not refine it here." Burgundy set the ingot down. "Build the refineries here. Build the processors here, and sell it finished, and keep the four times."

"Because that is not what we are." The King turned from the window. There was no heat in it. He said it the way a man states his own name. "We dig. We are very good at digging. We have been very good at digging for a long time, and it has kept this family alive, and a man who is good at one thing and reaches for a second thing usually loses the first. Leave the refineries to the men who own the refineries."

The minister had recovered himself and moved to fill the quiet, glad of ground he could stand on, and he began to explain the mechanics, the guarded processes, the foundries in distant systems, the machines that made the machines, all of it held off-world and held close, none of it for sale at any price. Burgundy stopped listening to the particular words. He had the shape of it already, and the shape assembled itself in him without being told, cold and complete, while the minister talked on.

Nobody on Dross could build a processor. Others controlled that, guarded it jealously. So Dross sold the flour and bought the bread, and this explained, finally, why his father was so aggressively averse to any kind of technological development on the planet. Why his "craft" was ruling men to mine year in and year out.

He said none of this out loud. He stood in the warm room with his hands going cold at his sides and understood that he was, at that moment, a kind of answer to his father's certainty, forty meters underground and forty kilometers from where the corvite came out of the earth, and that it was not an answer he had any intention of giving.

The minister was still going. Burgundy nodded in the right places until the King had had enough of the ledgers and put his hand on his son's shoulder, which he did rarely, and steered him back out into the cold.
He walked Burgundy to the statue.

His father had taken to this, giving the speech at the smallest opening. Burgundy could feel it coming the way you feel weather, the change in the man's breathing, the settling of his weight, and he set his face to receive it.
"You think I am hard," the King said. He was looking up at his own father's rusted, bleeding hand. "You have thought so since you were small. I know. I watched you decide it."
"No, sir."

"You did. It's all right." He was quiet a moment. "Look at him. He held this together in his time. His father before him. Mine after. We are not conquerors, Burgundy, we never were, whatever the sculptors want you to think. We are survivors. That is the whole of it. Do you know how hard it is to survive here."
"No, sir."

"No. You don't, and that is my doing, and I am not sorry for it." He gestured down the slope at the low city, the standing smoke, the rust. "This planet wants to kill the people on it. The cold wants to. The raiders in the systems around us would strip it to the rock if Nicholas's name did not sit over us like a roof, and Nicholas would strip it to the rock himself the day we came up short. And the men down there, the men who dig, they would burn the whole thing down some hard winter if they were ever allowed to gather and count how many of them there are against how few of us." He said it plainly, without alarm, a fact of the ledger like the take men. "That is what you are standing over. Everything that could go wrong here, at once, held off by hand, every day, for four generations. That is not cruelty. The watching, the control, the things you flinch at. It is the only thing between this family and the dark. You thread the needle. You keep the right men fed and the right men mining and you never let the two become the same men, and you do it every single day without rest, or one day it swallows you. And it will be you it swallows. When you are king."
He turned from the statue and looked at his son to see that the lesson had gone in.
Burgundy felt none of it.

That was the strange part, the part he could not have explained to his father if he had wanted to. Standing at the foot of the man who had held the line in his turn, hearing the whole case for the family laid out and every piece of it, he had to admit, probably true, he felt nothing lift in him. He felt cold. Not afraid, not moved. Cold, and tired, and aware of a pressure behind his ribs that had been building for weeks with nowhere to go, and that had lodged now, low and permanent, like a stone swallowed.

His father's world ran on keeping things small: men fed and never full, mining and never gathered, every warm room he had ever stood in paid for by a cold one below. Down there at night, with a disc in the reader and a machine getting better under his hands, nothing had to stay small for him to be warm. He had never put it in those words and did not put it in them now. He did not know what to do with it. He was seventeen and he did not have the shape of it yet. He only had the cold.
"Thank you, Father," he said.

They walked back across the square, the King's certainty going on ahead of him, sure of its ground, and Burgundy put his cold hands in his pockets and thought about the arm in the dark under a different building, that had learned that week to bring itself across the floor to the rock, and to hold what it found there exactly as hard as the thing would take.

chapters.title: chapter 12 The Craft
paragraphs: The days were the other craft, and his father had appointed himself its only honest teacher, and had grown generous with the lessons now that he believed his son was finally listening.
He learned the festivals.

This was the lesson that stayed with him longest. Twice a year, at New Year's and at the midsummer Descent, the King opened the storehouses. Alcohol for every workers' quarter, paid from the royal accounts. Three days of suspended shifts. Music, lanterns, the great drum lines that Burgundy had heard from the palace walls his whole childhood, a low thunder rolling up from the city that he had always assumed was simply what joy sounded like.

The midsummer Descent, his tutors had told him, went back to the Ghai, the mining people who had ruled Dross before his father's line, who marked the longest day by descending together into the oldest shaft to hang lanterns for their dead, to sing and drum and chant a cathartic chant and refusing to bring up a single stone, then followed by two days of feasting and lamp-lit processions, and folk music and spirit worship. Their marriages would happen during this festival.

And under the King's alcohol the Descent had an older fuel: something the elders drank from shallow cups that glowed faintly in the dark, a smell like hot metal and rain on road, passed hand to hand in the oldest rites.

Millions of people lived on Dross in conditions that anyone looking honestly would describe as slow grinding attrition, and twice a year the cities below the palace erupted into celebration so bright and loud it could be seen from orbit, and Burgundy had grown up believing this proved something about the spirit of the place.
It did prove something. He just had the something wrong.

He was at his father's side, eight months in, reviewing the festival provision, the King signing off on the alcohol allotments line by line, generous, unhurried, when his father said, without looking up:
"Do you know why I pay for this?"
"No, sir."

"Because a man who has something to look forward to does not burn down what he has." His father signed the last line. "Remember that. It is cheaper and more effective than the army, and it works better. Men do not rebel in the weeks before a festival. They do not rebel in the weeks after, while they are still telling stories about it. Time it right and you are never more than a few weeks from safety." He set down the pen. "That is the craft. Nobody will teach it to you honestly but me."
Burgundy nodded the way he had learned to nod.
It was the second time his father had walked him up to a working part of the thing and called it the craft. The statue had been the first. There would be more.

That night he went down through the old galleries and gave the arm harder work than a cup. He had taken the hand off it a week before and fitted a stub drill and a chisel point on a swap collar, so the arm could bore or split and choose between them, and he had set a fist of corvite on the sled's reach, knocked loose from the old gallery wall. Corvite did not forgive. Cut it square and it came away clean. Cut it two degrees off and it burst into worthless grit. The arm read the face, set the drill to it, and took a core out of the block without shattering it, and dropped the core in the tray, and went back for the next bite on its own.

Then he taught it to grade itself. He wrote it two numbers to keep: how deep each cut ran, and how much charge the servos burned to move a kilogram of rock. It logged them every pass. And because he had also given it room to change one small thing between passes and keep whichever number came back better, it began, in the smallest way, to improve without him. He watched it try a shallower approach angle, log the burn, keep the angle. Try a slower feed, log the depth, keep the feed. By the fourth night it was cutting corvite two degrees cleaner than the code he had given it, and the two degrees were its own.

And then it stopped getting better. He added a sensor to the drill head and it climbed a little and flattened. He rewrote the scoring function and it climbed a little and flattened. He sat on the cold floor and looked at the log leveling off, and understood the shape of it, and it was his own shape. The machine could keep whichever small change came back better, but it could not find a change he had not already built it the room to try. Every real step still came off his bench: his read of the log, his rewrite, his upload, carried down in the two or three hours a night the day-prince could spare. He had made a thing that improved itself and put a ceiling on it in the same stroke, and the ceiling was one exhausted boy with two lives. He turned the drill collar out of the arm and set it back, and went up to sleep.

chapters.title: chapter 13 The Preserve
paragraphs: They went out into the preserve in the high days of the Midsummer, the festival season, when the sun stood over the hills and would not come down and the brush country lay hot and dry under it. The keepers were already ahead of them in the shimmer, walking the far grass, scattering grain for the animals to come and find.

Burgundy carried something private out into the heat. The arm had run the whole of the night before without him standing over it, and had still been running when he climbed the stair to sleep, and the thought of it working down there in the cool dark, getting a little better on its own, stayed with him the whole way out to the blind. It was the one good thing in his hands.

His father had never taken him to the preserve. That was its own kind of promotion, and Burgundy read it as one. Ever since the lecture, ever since the boy had bent into the shape the King wanted, the King had taken to handing him the inheritance in pieces, any hour he could get one in. A few sentences in a corridor. A ledger turned around on the table so the son could follow a column down. Now the preserve, which the King's grandfather had walled off from the works a lifetime ago: a strip of fast brush country kept green and warm through the freeze on fuel that would have heated a quarter of the low city.

They went out before the light was full. The party was small. The King, and Burgundy, and a governor of one of the western works, a broad comfortable man named Hald who laughed a beat ahead of his own jokes. And two ministers. An old one from the treasury who said next to nothing and coughed into a glove. And the security minister, Osk, a soft heavy man with a mild face and quiet hands, whom Burgundy had watched across the council table for years and never once heard raise his voice.

The blind was a low stone wall at the near edge of a clearing, mossed, older than any of them, built for this and nothing else. The keepers had gone out ahead in the dark and scattered feed across the open ground, pale grain in a wide arc thirty meters off the wall. The men settled behind the stone on cushions a servant had carried out, and went quiet, and waited, and the animals came.

They came the way a stabled horse comes to a bucket. Fen-buck, Hald called them, though Burgundy had only ever seen the word in a book: dun, heavy through the shoulder, the size of a yearling calf, bred inside the wall for four generations and fed by hand their whole lives. They had no more fear of a man behind a wall than a dog has of the hand that fills its dish. They stepped out of the brush into the open, put their heads down to the scattered grain, and ate.

The King shot the first one. It dropped where it stood, over the feed, and the others did not bolt. That was the part Burgundy could not stop watching. They lifted their heads at the sound and looked for a moment and then went back down to the grain. A second wandered out of the brush to join them. Hald took it, and laughed, and reached for his flask.
"Your turn, prince," the King said.

Burgundy shot one. Nothing about it was hard. The animal stood thirty meters off with its head down and did not run, and he brought it down, and the ones around it looked up and looked back and went on eating, and he felt the men behind him warm to him, and he set the thing aside and did not want to lift it again.
"We'll want more men," Osk said then, to the clearing, to no one. "Hald's been saying it a year and he's right. We're stretched thin."
"Thin against what," Burgundy said.

"Everything the winter throws up. We're standing two new barracks near the southern complexes before the Descent, and I'll be honest with you, prince, I could fill them twice over and still be short of where I'd like to be." He said it comfortably, a man discussing a harvest. "There are challenges coming. There always are. The trick is to be standing ahead of them and not behind."
"What challenges." Burgundy kept his voice in the flat register the room had taught him. "Is someone coming for Dross? Off the lanes?"

It was the King who answered that, without turning his head, watching the grain. "The outside is Nicholas's affair. It always has been. The army has never once fired on a thing that came out of the sky, and it never will. That is not its work."
"Then what is its work."

Osk warmed to it, the way another man warms to a subject he has thought about alone for years and rarely gets to say aloud. "Order," he said, as though it were both obvious and a little sad that it had to be spoken. "You would be surprised, prince, how thin the thing is that keeps all these people fed and housed and breathing out here. It holds because it holds. Let a few loud men talk a shaft into believing it can do better, and the shaft stops, and then the one next to it stops, and inside a month you have a district that cannot feed itself and will not go down, and the collection comes on schedule regardless. I have seen where that road ends. I have been the man who had to walk it back." He said it the way another man might describe pulling a child out of a road.

A third fen-buck stepped from the brush. Hald swung toward it, missed his own timing, laughed, and took it on the second attempt. "Ungrateful is what they are," he said, wiping his mouth. "You want to know my trouble, prince? Half my belt hours go to picking waste rock out of the quota. They pad it. Cut a ton of stone with the ore just to make the number and let my pickers sort it, and then they've the nerve to send a man round asking after the stipend. Wants a firm hand, the whole southern belt. Always has."
The treasury minister coughed into his glove. "A firm hand is cheaper than a full one," he said, and said nothing else the rest of the morning.

"You see, they hear it wrong," Osk went on, gentle, undeterred, as if correcting a kind misunderstanding. "They think the man behind the wall is against them. He isn't. A man alone with a grievance is only ever a danger to himself. The kindest thing you can do for him is see that he never finds the others who feel the same, because the day three of them find each other is the day it stops being a grievance and starts being a committee, and a committee you cannot walk back the gentle way." He shot as he said it, easily, without breaking his sentence, and a fourth animal folded over the feed. "People call the early work hard. It isn't hard. It's mercy, done in time, before it has to be done late and in the open where everyone has to watch."
"There's been another," the King said, mild, to his son, a teaching note in it. "Tell him, Osk."

"The third this year," Osk said. "A drying shed in the southern quarter. Men meeting after the shift, in the dark, where the pump noise covers a voice. The word committee had come up." He let the word sit. Burgundy had learned in his years of council that it was the one word this room feared past all others. "Six taken. Quietly. His Majesty's judgment, and the right one, was to keep it quiet, with the Descent only five weeks off. Quiet plus a festival bleeds the pressure better than any lesson made in daylight." He said it lightly. But under the lightness Burgundy heard the thing Osk was working not to say, and half heard himself, that it was the third in a year, that they were finding one another faster than the drums and the free drink could talk them apart.

Burgundy sat behind the wall with the grain spread in front of him and the soft words going past him and did the translation without deciding to, the way he now translated everything said in that room. Domestic disputes meant strikes. Groups meant men gathered after a shift to say aloud that the stipend did not cover the winter. Committee meant men deciding a thing together instead of one at a time, and being taken for it in the dark. Pacification and repair had been a line in a ledger since before he was born, from the eleven days the southern shafts would not go down and the army went into the workers' quarter and came out again. Three thousand men in barracks at the shaft heads, and not one of them had ever stood against a thing from off the planet, because the enemy the army had been built for had always been the people who dug. The army was a fence, and the fence faced inward. It stood there to keep the miners mining and frightened and apart. And Osk, who had scattered no grain with his own two hands and would tell you plainly he had scattered none, believed all the way to the floor of himself that the fence was a kindness.

Out in the clearing a fifth fen-buck stepped from the brush, unhurried, incurious, and put its head down to the grain the keepers had thrown wide to bring it to exactly that spot, and the King, unhurried, shot it. Burgundy watched the others near it lift their heads at the sound and settle and go on feeding, and he thought of the storehouses that opened twice a year, the drums, the free drink carried out into the quarters by the cartload, and of grain thrown wide to bring a thing calm and unafraid to the one place the wall was waiting.

Some days, that was the hardest part of the whole performance, not the pretending, but the learning. His father was a careful ruler. That was the thing Burgundy had not expected. The cruelty was craft, as his father always said, refined over generations, applied with patience. The festivals, the army, the tribute, the shaved stipends. It all fit together, it all worked, and his father moved through it with the fluency of a man who had genuinely mastered his inheritance. Burgundy sat at his left hand and nodded and learned the craft of ruling men, and told himself he was learning it as reconnaissance, and was never fully sure this was true.

He got through the rest of the morning. He shot two more, because it would have been noticed if he had not. When they rode back the light was already sliding off the hills, and his father was pleased with him, easy in the saddle, telling a story about the grandfather and the walling of the preserve that Burgundy did not hear a word of.

That night he did not go down to the white room. There was nothing down there that could take the weight of what he had brought back off the field. The hand that closed its grip and held was no help to him now. He went up instead, the other way, toward the library and the turned-down lamps and the deep shelves and the yellow book, and his mother, who was the one person in the palace he could say it to.

chapters.title: chapter 14 What the Library Was For
paragraphs: His mother was where she always was after dark, at the long oiled table at the bottom of the wing, in a pool of light thrown by a single reading lamp turned low. The library ran three stories up into the dark over her head and two more below, ten thousand spines gone to shadow on their iron walkways, and she had lit exactly one lamp, the way she always did, enough to read by and no more. Farther out among the stacks a few lanterns burned in their brackets, small and yellow, marking the crossings. The rest was black. It was the only room in the palace built by his mother's family, and the only room his father had not entered in nineteen years, because his father was not curious. So it was the one place under the whole roof where a thing could be said out loud and stay.

She looked up when his lamp came down the spiral stair, and she watched him cross the floor, and she set her pen down before he reached the table. She had always known what he was carrying before he said it. He had gotten that from her.
"You went to the preserve," she said.
"You know I did."
"How many did he kill."
"I lost count." He stayed standing. "That isn't what I came to say."
She folded her hands and waited. She did not tell him to sit. She let a person arrive at his own speed, and she did not fill the quiet for him.
So he let it out.

He told her about the wall. A low stone berm at the edge of a clearing, a blind they had built and kept mowed, and behind it the King and two ministers and a governor with cups of something hot, waiting. He told her how the animals came. Pale, long-legged things the preserve kept for no purpose but this, walking out of the brush into the open to feed, unhurried, because nothing in that clearing had ever hurt them until the second it did. His father shot, and the animal would fold at the knees, and the loaders would go out and drag it back, and the talk would not even stop for it.
"And they talked," he said. "The whole morning. About the army."
Mira said nothing.

"There are going to be more men in the barracks next year. I asked what for. I thought, invasion, raiders, Nicholas. The security minister looked at me like I was simple. Nicholas is the sky, he said. The army is for the ground." Burgundy heard his own voice climbing and did not stop it. "He has words for it. They all do. Domestic disputes. Pacification. When men gather in a shed at night and talk about their stipend, that's a committee, and a committee gets taken, quietly, before the festival, so the drums can bleed off what's left. He said it the way you'd talk about weather. He reloaded while he said it."
He put his hands flat on the table.

"They shot animals that walked into the open because they were bred not to know better. And in between, they talked about doing the same thing to the people in the shafts. Wait for them to gather where you can see them. Take them. And it isn't even cruelty, that's what I can't hold. He isn't a cruel man. He thinks he's a gardener."
Then he asked her the thing he had come down the stair to ask.

"You've been here nineteen years." He said it evenly, which cost him. "You see all of it. You've seen it longer than I've been alive. The blood goes up the ramp in casks and you sign for it in your own hand. So how. How have you let this happen. All this time, in this room, with all of this." He put his hand out at the dark, the walkways, the ten thousand books, the yellow spine somewhere above them in the shadow. "How do you sit here and let it run."

She let the question stand in the lamplight a long time. She did not reach for it the way he wanted her to, fast, defensive. She looked at him the way she looked at a manifest that had come in wrong, reading it all the way down before she spoke.
"You think I chose this," she said. "You've decided I sat down in this chair nineteen years ago and chose it."
"I think you could have."

"I was your age," she said. "I was seventeen. I was put on a ship and sent to a man I had never met, on a planet I had seen only in survey photographs, because my family needed the trade and I was the price of it. I asked for one thing. I asked for this wing. And your grandfather gave it to me, because a wing full of books is a cheap way to keep a bride quiet, and your father has not opened its door since, because he decided long ago that whatever I do in here is harmless." She turned the pen a quarter-turn on the table, and set it straight. "That is the whole of the power I was handed, Burgundy. A locked room he does not bother to unlock. Tell me what you would have overthrown from inside it."
He did not answer.

"It is more complicated than you think," she said. "I know that is the sentence every comfortable person says to every angry young one, and I know how it sounds. Hear it anyway. Your father is a jailer. He is also not lying about the sky. Nicholas is real. The raiders are real. There are six systems of men who would come down on this planet and strip it to the rock if the grey ships stopped coming, and they would not pause to explain it in gentle words first. Some of the fear he sells is a lie he tells to keep men in the shafts. And some of it is the truth, and he has built a life out of knowing exactly which parts are which. That is his craft. You have been learning the same distinction all season, whether you meant to or not."
"So you did nothing," he said, but it had less in it now.

"I did what the room allowed." She said it without heat. "A disc in a servant's basket. A better pump to a village that had been carrying water in its arms. A boy in a workers' quarter who can read now, because a reader reached him, and who will teach three more. Small things. Slow things. I have been leaking this planet its own future by the thimbleful for nineteen years, because a thimble was what I could move without his noticing, and a thimble that arrives beats a flood that gets you hanged." She stopped. "It was never going to be me. I always knew that. I was the wing. I was the crates coming in. I was never going to be the thing the crates were for."

She stood. She came around the table, into the small lamp, and for once she did not look like the queen at council or the woman signing manifests on the field. She looked at him the way she had looked at him the first morning, at the top of the ladder, with her hand on the yellow book.

"And then you started taking the clocks apart," she said. "When you were eight. And I watched you, for ten years, become the one thing this room was built to make and never managed to. All of it. The wing, the routes, the discs, nineteen years of thimbles. It was the long way around to a person who could do what I couldn't." Her voice did not rise. "You are not learning your father's craft as reconnaissance and hoping that's true. I am telling you it's true. Whatever you build in that room, whatever you decide to do with it, I will treat as my own work. It is my own work. It has my whole life in it."
"I haven't decided to do anything," he said. "I don't have a plan. I came down here because I couldn't stand it. That's all this is."

"I know." She put her hand against the side of his face, briefly, the way she almost never did. "You don't have to have a plan tonight. But hear the other half of it, so it's said, and then we don't have to say it again." She let the hand fall. "When you do decide. Whatever it is. I have more than a wing to give you. I have a family across nine systems that will move anything for a price and ask nothing after, and that owes me, and that has never once been afraid of your father or his sky. Whatever it takes, Burgundy. I mean the words. Whatever it takes."

He did not know what she was offering. That was the thing he carried back up the stair afterward, heavier than the grievance he had brought down. He had come to say he hated the shape of the world, the way a boy says it, wanting only to be heard. And his mother had heard him, and had answered him like someone laying a tool on the bench for a job not yet named, and he did not know the size of the tool, and he was fairly sure she had not told him the half of what she meant.

chapters.title: chapter 15 Mira's Shipment
paragraphs: One night in the ninth month, the white room had to wait.
Mira was standing in the vast library when Burgundy arrived.
"Tonight you need to come with me. I need to show you."
"Show me what?"
"Just come."
He did not ask again
They walked through the palace the predictable way.
"does father know--" Burgundy started.
"Yes" She cut him off. "This is a part of your princely duties."
Soon they were outside walking toward the north gate.
"So, how's it going?" Mira asked
They had not talked about the white room since the night she had showed it to him. Burgundy assumed that she was asking about what he had been doing in there.
"Good. I've just been reading. There's so much to read."
"Good." She said, indicating the conversation was over.

They arrived to the north gate where a guard opened it without looking at either of them, then along a path running east, toward the low ground beyond the cargo field where the tribute loaded. Burgundy had assumed ships came down on Dross in exactly one place. But he had been wrong.
There was a second field. Smaller. Lit only by amber lamps set low along its edges. A freight ship sat on the landing pad, dark except for a few small utility lights no bigger than lamp-wicks.
This was not one of Nicholas's grey giants, which never landed at all. This was much smaller, maybe 10% the size. It was scuffed, patched, resting on wheels. Its cargo ramp was down.
The loaders rolled crates up the ramp on low sleds.
Burgundy and Mira approached the ramp just as a woman was walking down it out of the ship to meet them. She was carrying a clipboard under her  arm.  Was this Ressa, his mother's cousin?

She held the slate out to Mira. "Manifest's ready. Ressa signed the outbound this afternoon.  The medicine order is short two pallets. The vendor's problem, not ours." So this wasn't Ressa, but rather one of her people.  His mother's cousin ran the trade without attending it. Then, with a glance at Burgundy that lasted no more than a half a second the woman said, "is this–"
"Yes" Mira said.
The woman snuck one more glance at Burgundy then turned back up the ramp signaling to the loaders to proceed.
Mira began focusing on the papers on the clipboard, scanning each line and occasionally signing her name.
Burgundy watched the ship.

Up the ramp went the crates of ore. He knew it by the markings now: density codes, grade markings, black corvite in sealed bundles. And beside the ore, in a separate stack the crews handled differently, more slowly, in padded cradles: casks. Small. Banded with metal. When a loader tilted one to seat it on the sled, the seam of the lid showed a faint glow, cold and steady.

He knew what it was. He had heard the word over the years. Mostly in a whisper: Cinder. A mind altering drug. The substance that fueled the spiritual dimension of the midsummer Descent. Refined from a rare deep seam mineral called Cindrite in a method the Ghai discovered. Fleks of the purified metal were ground with the tunnel mushroom and then consumed as a tea that glowed pale blue. Cinder was sacred in the old ritual but illegal in every system. And yet there was a black market for it throughout the whole galaxy. It was a stimulant that ran a man for two days and gave him blissful visions. This was Dross's second harvest, their metal cash crop that funded the Kings vanity projects, ~~now flowing up a ramp in casks bound for the black market run by his mother's family.~~

And down the ramp came the arriving cargo. Burgundy had expected the incoming cargo to be illicit items like drugs or weapons. But instead he saw seed stock in heavy sacks. Casks of cooking oil, sacks of grain marked in a language he couldn't read. But also luxury items for the palace. Cooler crates likely full of special meats from other worlds. This stuff would end up on his plate at dinner. He had never wonder its origins.

after an hour of loaders going back and forth he saw a familiar stack of boxes of all sizes: Coils of special wire, drill heads wrapped in oiled paper, motors the size of fists nested in foam and what he craved most: the small wooden boxes he knew contained crystal discs from the Core world, packed tightly between wool and sawdust.

It was worrisome to have it all out in the open like this. The crew carrying his secret down the ramp on dollys like any other shipment. But when he really thought about it, he realized that to them this was just another crate. It may look suspicious to his father, but His father didn't ever come to these shipments. According to Mira, he hadn't for years. He preferred Mira to be the interface.
Mira looked at one of the crew and said "Lew." and nodded her head at the bundle of Burgundy's items.
Lew must have been the insider that Mira paid to get all this from the cargo field to the white room behind the bookshelf. He had no idea what kind of arrangement they had but he trusted it was safe.
Lew gave almost no acknowledgment that he had heard but went straight to gather the boxes and crates onto a motorized loader, and off he went into the dark.

Mira was finishing on the clipboard now. She initialed a line. She stopped at another. "This count is wrong. there were only 17 casks." The woman on the ramp checked; agreed. Mira corrected it herself, small precise figures, the same hand that labeled the toolbox drawers in the white room.

chapters.title: chapter 16 DREKKO
paragraphs: Nearly a year in, the nights turned from studying discs to actually building.

The hardware changed everything. The processors from Mira's tables ran his feedback code four hundred times faster than the salvaged board in his first prototype; simulations that had taken a night now took a minute, which meant he could be wrong four hundred times as often. The crates brought hydraulics of a kind Dross's own industry had never seen,  sealed actuators, compact and strong enough to put three tons of pressure through a joint the size of his fist. They brought strain sensors finer than anything in the mines, servo assemblies, spun-carbon frame stock that weighed a third of the salvaged loader steel.

this made building easy by comparison. Like putting together a puzzle. And By 14 months behind the yellow book, there were three prototypes of his drilling robot. He started calling a name, like his second mother used to do.
And he chose something inspired by the last name of the one of the Core world authors he read name Karz Dreck. He started calling his robot a DREKKO.

They stood in a row along the white room's western wall. They were a total rebuild and redesign of the robot he had shown his father. No more single fat wheel from a serving cart. Instead, each unit now ran on a pair of independently driven treaded tracks that could soften or stiffen on command, his old sleeve-and-compressor trick, rebuilt with real components, so that the machines climbed the dungeon stairs behind him with a rocking, patient  easy gait.

Each carried twin drill arms on hydraulic mounts. But they were more than drills. He had requested a disc containing everything the Central Library had on the history of manual mining techniques which he used to design arms that could rotate between a cutting head, a chisel point for splitting along a seam, a blunt hammer face for shattering, a scaling claw for raking loose rock off the ceiling before it fell on its own, and a flat scraper for cleaning a face down to bare mineral.
Slung between the tracks rode the sorting bucket, and beside it a small grading screen that shook waste from ore as the machine worked.
And in the DREKKO's chests behind green glass, the advanced processors ran his code.
He had coded the whole things, especially the feedback system based on what the discs taught him.
"Mining is a delicate art. Drill, pick, or chisel, each to its moment, the whole skill of it being to take the ore clean and waste nothing."  said one of the old books he read off his screen.
The machines scored their own work now on key things like depth of cut, energy spent per kilogram.

He had sat through a council session where a regional governor, a man who ran one of the distribution centers, complained at length about waste rock. The miners, he said, padded their quotas with rock they harvested that was not ore, and his belts and pickers spent half their hours separating. His father had promised stricter foremen.
That night, Burgundy added a new measure to the feedback system: waste ratio, the fraction of worthless rock in everything the machine cut. The DREKKOS could measure and report this now.
They were, by any measure that had existed on Dross a year ago, marvels.

But Burgundy could only go so far without putting the DREKKOS to use. He found a door in the underground portion of his mothers library that was sealed and painted over. When he pried it open he found a hall to an old dungeon and a gallery of prison cells centuries abandoned.

Wondering through these old cells, he quickly noticed that he was surrounded by veins of mineral. The palace's foundations sat directly on the shoulder of the southern ore country, and somewhere in the centuries, when power shifted hands, the new ruler had built the palace atop an old mine. There was still unmined riches here. Burgundy had tested the rock. And the sensor had come back with a reading he made it repeat three times.
Corvite.
A seam of it, thick as a room. A mineral that probably wasn't valuable when this was an active dungeon. It was, he understood, a small fortune sitting inside the palace's own foundations.

It was also, more usefully, the perfect teacher for his robots. Corvite was the hardest ore on Dross: dense, brittle in the wrong ways, prone to shattering into worthless gravel if the cutting angle was wrong by even a few degrees. The southern shafts lost more men to corvite seams than to any other work. If the machines could learn corvite, they could mine anything on the planet.
So every night, after council, after the coat came off, Burgundy went down through the old dungeons and set the three prototypes against the wall, and watched them try.

He moved his terminal and array screens from the white room to this dungeon-turned testing room so he could work down there and watch the robots try to cut into the rock. There was something comforting about being back in a basement working on robots again.

The DREKKOs tried their hand at real rock for the first time. They were not failing, exactly. That was what made it hard. Each unit could bore into the seam. Each could strip freed ore into its bucket, sort waste rock by density. Watching them work, a foreman from the southern shafts would have wept. three machines chewing steadily into the hardest ore on the planet.

But the pace was wrong. He clocked them against the numbers he now knew from council: a good southern crew, twelve miners with picks and a blast allotment, pulled roughly a ton of raw corvite in a shift, losing a third of it to shatter. His three machines together managed perhaps half that, losing a quarter. Better per machine than a man. Not better enough.

At this rate, replacing one shaft's full crews would take hundreds of machines, and he could build, with every disc and every crate and every stolen midnight hour, perhaps one every few months. It would be years.

And they did not improve themselves the way he dreamed they would.  The discs painted a theoretical picture of robots that with the right sensors and right code could learn from its mistakes, and that was the true wall.

His code let each machine rate itself and even automatically make small improvements, by itself, a better angle here, a smarter torque curve there, but the tuning flattened out. Each prototype would improve for a week, ten days, and then settle onto a plateau, grinding away at the seam with a competence that never became mastery.

He would adjust the code, or add more sensors and the machine would climb a little, and plateau again. But he, once again, was the bottleneck. Every real improvement still ran through him: his diagnosis, his rewrite, his upload. Three machines waiting on one exhausted seventeen-year-old's judgment, and the seventeen-year-old was spending his days nodding at tribute ledgers.
18 months. Three machines, and a plateau he could not code his way past.

Some nights he sat on the cold floor of his prison lab with his back against the old cell bars, the notebooks piled beside him, the green panels pulsing their patient rhythm against the dark, and closed his eyes, mapping out the whole thing again in his head. All the theoretical math the smartest minds in the galaxy had published promising code and hardware that would learn and grow like a human brain.  It never did.

What he had built was remarkable but insufficient. And he had begun to suspect, in the grey hours when the drum of the drills  and chisels blurred into the sound of his own pulse, that no amount of his own cleverness would close the gap. He could not think fast enough to set these three machines free to think for themselves.

chapters.title: chapter 17 The Bridge
paragraphs: It began on a spring morning, 20 months after his mother first swung open the bookcase, and it began the way every important thing in Burgundy's life had begun: disguised as an ordinary day.

The day was worse than ordinary in fact. It was mundane in the specific, grinding way that palace days could be mundane: a morning council about grain storage, a midday audience with a delegation of northern foremen whose grievance took two hours to state and one sentence to deny, an afternoon review of festival provisioning that his father conducted line by line, signature by signature, while intracate colored light from a massive window moved slowly across the flagstones on the council chamber floor.

Burgundy sat through all of it. He nodded in the right places. He had been nodding in the right places for almost 2 years now, and the nodding had become so automatic that he sometimes caught himself doing it alone, at night, at his workbench, agreeing with no one.
The whole day, one thought occupied his mind.
The discs.

His mother had delivered him a new crate the week before, and he quickly saw that this batch was different. He had known it was different by the third page of the first disc. Reading off his screen after jamming the disc into his terminal one evening, coat still on, he read, standing up. It was 12 new papers with several major breakthroughs.

Core-world teams in top labs, three of them, working the same problem from different directions had begun successfully testing robotics whose own sensors fed the machine's own learning. Every strain gauge and thermal reading and torque curve pouring data into the code's scoring functions in real time, the way a hot lantern teaches a child's hand: touch it once, and the brain rewrites itself so you never touch it again. Core world engineers were showing robots and code could do this.  The papers called it "closed-loop embodiment algorithms."
And the night before this spring day, Burgundy had read all twelve papers, three times each til he could see the code in his sleep.
but the more he read, the more he started to see gaps.  Things that were obvious to him but that the Core world researchers somehow missed.

And that's when it hit him The papers were brilliant but they were partially blind. Each team had proved you could teach a robot to improve itself. But they did so in simulation, on a simple rig, in a lab scrubbed clean of the things that made his machines choke, the real world Dust, heat, physics.
And as he read the same three authors arguing past one another, he saw that none of them had ever spent a night on their backs under a machine with sealant on their hands.

The real applications were apparently beneath the math, or beyond it, or simply invisible to men who had never held a tool. And Burgundy, reading in a stolen room, on a backwater planet, with grease under his nails and years of failure, understood something that surprised him: He knew things they did not.
He saw solutions that they could only argue about with vague words and concepts like *"...real-world industrial application scenarios"*. He was...ahead of them.
He got back to the white room that evening before the lamps in the workers' quarter came on, and he worked.
Something had shifted in his mind. A confidence that he was not just learning from the core world engineers, he was competing with them.

He could feel that he was arriving to potentially the final frontier to making the robot teach itself:  the sensor buses that fed data from his robots arms to its brain had been built, by him, in a different life, to report their readings on a fixed cycle to a fixed log.

But now the learning loop needed them raw and constant, like a firehose instead of a faucet, a waterfall of real time data. So with a few lines of code and some rewiring, he opened them up. As constant as human senses flowing into a brain.
But every time he opened the data channels all the way, the processors drowned. The scoring functions fell behind the sensations they were supposed to score.

The machines got clumsy, worse than before, drunk on their own feeling, and twice that night a drill arm slammed a cutting head into the corvite at an angle that sent shatter pinging off the gallery walls like shrapnel.
He had to replace a drill arm, twice that night. Something he had done 20 times by now.

He tried throttling the flow. He tried batching it. He tried letting the machine choose its own sampling rate, which the second paper hinted at and the third paper warned against, and the warning proved correct in a way that cost him a hydraulic line and an hour on his back under the second prototype with a mix of sealant and lubricant on his hands.

By the fifth hour of the night he had stopped being methodical. He knew he had stopped and he let it happen. There was a mode he went into, past a certain hour, that he did not entirely trust and could not entirely do without, where the experiments stopped being designed and started being thrown.
He recoded and rewired the sensor buses on all three machines in  different configurations. He wrote eighteen scoring variants and qued them up to run in sequence.

He gave them access  to the micro-charge dispensers he had mounted on their arms a month earlier. These were little explosives the size of beads, dispensed from magazines within the robots' arms. He had never used them before, they were meant for an experiment in pre-fracturing the rock, but he had shelved the idea as too dangerous to automate.
But tonight he was letting everything fly. He set bounds on the charges. He checked the bounds twice to make sure he wasn't about to blow up the whole foundation of the castle.

Then he lined the three DREKKOs up against the seam which was punctuated by a shallow tunnel after over a year of their patient, insufficient chewing, and he loaded the whole reckless suite of experiments into the queue, every variant, every configuration, set to run in rotation, each machine scoring itself and passing what it learned sideways to the other two.
He looked up, and the high thin slit window of the cell was illuminating with a warm sharp light.
Dawn. He had done it again. Council was in two hours and he had not slept in, he counted, twenty-six hours. He had to press go on this flurry of code and machinery and leave.
Wash, coat, council, foremen, docks. The tribute came down today.
He looked at the three machines idling against the black seam, their green panels pulsing, the experiment queue loaded and waiting on his word.
"Go," he said to himself and pressed one button on his keyboard and left them working..

He did not look back at the wall. If he had, there would have been nothing to see. It looked like every other morning he had left them: three patient machines, a barely wounded vein, a boy going up the old stairs two at a time with his coat over his arm.
Council was a blur

He got through the grain reports. He got through a dispute between two southern governors . Twice his head dipped, the full nod, chin to chest, and the second time he came back from it to find the room silent and his father looking at him down the length of the table.
"Am I boring you," the King said.
"No, sir. I apologize. I was reading late."
"Reading."
"The northern field reports." The lie arrived without being sent for. Two years of practice.
His father studied him a moment longer. "Read earlier," he said, and turned back to the table, and Burgundy exhaled through his nose, slowly, the way you let pressure out of a line.

The main business of the council was "groups." which was the royalty euphemism for gatherings of disgruntled citizens who were discussing strike or rebellion or anything of the sort.    There had been "groups" in the workers' quarters. Secret ones, at night, in the drying sheds and the pump rooms, the third such network broken up in a year. The word *strike* had been used; the interior minister said the word *organizer*, which Burgundy had learned in almost two years of council was the word this room feared most.

Six men had been taken. The minister recommended, and the King approved, that the taking be kept quiet, because with the festival five weeks out, quiet plus festival would bleed the pressure better than any public lesson.

"They are tired," the King said, sighing. "Tired men make threats in sheds. Then the drums start and the drink is poured, and they remember they have something to lose, and they lose interest in losing it." he chuckled to himself, apparently bemused by his turn of phrase.
He set down the pen and looked, briefly, at his son, a teaching look, checking that the lesson had landed. Burgundy nodded.

But something in his chest had leaned forward, listening, because there was something new in what the minister had said: six men taken, a third network in a year, the pressure rising faster than festivals could bleed it.

The tribute came down at midday, and Burgundy stood on the observation platform at his father's right hand and watched, as he had watched every month for almost two years, and it had never once stopped being the most alien thing he had ever seen.

Nicholas's ships did not land. That was the first thing about them, the thing that reorganized your understanding of what a ship was. They arrived out of the white sky, three of them today, each the length of the palace and its grounds laid end to end, and they stopped, and hung, a hundred meters above the cargo field, without wings, without any visible negotiation with gravity.

Their hulls were the grey of deep water and utterly unmarked, and they made a sound that was less a sound than a pressure, a low field of force that Burgundy felt in his molars and in the bones of his chest, and that made the whole field of stacked crates, ten thousand tonnes of ore, graded, weighed, sealed, a month of the planet's blood in boxes, look like an offering laid out of fear. which is what it was.
Then the arms came down.

They unfolded from the bellies of the ships in silence, joint after joint after joint, white and precise, each one long enough to reach from the palace gate to the throne, and they began to pick up the crates. thirty-tonne crates rising in gentle clusters, drawn up into holds that never showed their insides. Nicolas's soldiers  stood on the field in their painted safety rings and watched, hard men with hooks on their belts.

The platform behind them held the usual small group of nobels: two regional governors in grey coats, the tribute master with his ledger men, a colonel of the domestic army standing where he could watch both the loading and the crowd that watched it.
Burgundy was so tired that the membrane between his two lives had gone thin, and the day-prince stood on the platform in his coat while the night-builder counted joints, estimated torque
He could not help it.
If those arms had a feedback loop, he thought, they would teach themselves to sort mid-air, to nest the ascending clusters tighter, to shave a second off every lift and then a second off the shaving.

The thought belonged to the night. And behind it, because he was too tired to keep the two rooms separate, sat the machines he had left against the seam that morning, and the small bright hope that the explsoives had not brought the castle down on them.
His head dipped.

He caught it, half a second, no more, and came back to the pressure-hum and the white sky, and found his father looking at him. Not with anger. That was the strange thing. The King had seen the dip, and something in his face was almost soft.
"You're tired," the King said, quietly, under the hum.
"Yes, sir."
His father turned back to the field, to the last crates rising into the grey hulls, and he was silent for a while, and then he said, still watching the ships:

"You've become a great prince. I want you to know I see it. You'll be king someday, sooner than either of us would like, the way the years are going, and for the first time I believe you're ready for it. More than ready." He paused. The arms folded themselves away, joint after joint, into the bellies of the massive ships. "I'm glad you gave up those childish things. The toys, the wires. I know it wasn't easy, but look at you." He nodded at the field, at the order of it, at the month's blood rising into the sky on schedule. "This suits you. This is right for you. This is what you are."
The ships went up without seeming to move, the way the sun crosses a sky, and were gone, and the pressure lifted out of Burgundy's molars, and the field was just a field again, emptied.
"Thank you, Father," Burgundy said.
It was, he reflected, walking off the platform at his father's side, the kindest thing his father had ever said to him.

He was released from his duties an hour before dusk. by the time he reached the last of his three routes through the old galleries he was running, coat over his arm, taking the worn stairs down in the dark by memory.
He smelled it before he saw it.

Rock dust. In the hallway. thick. Not the ordinary haze the prototypes raised in a night's work, a thickness in the air of the hall of the old jail cells, a mineral fog that hung in the light of his lamp, and under it a smell he knew from exactly one place in his life: the rim of a working shaft. Blasting residue. Deep rock, opened.
He came around the last turn into the cell-turned-lab and stopped.
The wall was gone.

chapters.title: chapter 18 Tunnels
paragraphs: Not damaged. Not advanced upon. *Gone*.

Where the seam had been, where almost two years of patient insufficient chewing had left a shallow scarred tunnel there was now a hole. A real tunnel. Round-shouldered, clean-walled, taller than he was, driven straight into the rock, and so deep that his lamp simply failed inside it, the light falling into the dark the way a stone falls into a well.
The three prototypes were nowhere to be found.

Burgundy stood at the mouth of the tunnel for a long moment, listening to his own pulse beating in his neck, and then he did the thing that almost two years of discipline had built into him: he went to the terminal.
The logs were still streaming across all three screens.

He read standing up, then sitting, then leaning into the screen with both hands on the desk, scrolling, not breathing right. The queue of reckless experiments had run in rotation, as designed, for the first two hours after he had left, variant after variant failing in the old familiar ways, drowned processors, drunk actuators, one logged shatter-event that had cost the second prototype a cutting edge. And then, in the third hour, one configuration on the third machine, one of the ones he had wired past midnight and could barely remember, had *caught*.

Caught was the only word for it. He watched it in the logs the way you watch a spark take in dry grass. The data firehose and the scoring loop had synchronized. Not throttled, not batched, but brought into rhythm, the machine sampling its own body in rhythm with its own actions, feeling each cut as it made the cut, and the performance line, flat for almost two years, had bent upward. Then the third machine had passed the configuration sideways to the other two, as designed, and all three lines had bent, and then the loop had begun doing the thing the papers promised could happen but never achieved outside a lab, and Burgundy had never once seen with his own eyes:
It improved the improving.

Every second, the logs said, each machine was taking in its thousands of tiny sensations, torque flutter, thermal bloom, the acoustic signature of rock about to shatter versus rock about to yield, and converting them into micro-adjustments: a cutting angle shaved by a tenth of a degree, a charge from the micro-dispensers placed not where the rock was weakest but where the *next three cuts* would want it weakened, the blast so small and so exact that it did the work of an hour's grinding in a sound no louder than a knuckle crack. And each adjustment fed the next. And the rate of adjustment was itself adjusting. The performance curve in the logs was no longer a line bending. It was a line skyrocketing up.
He looked at the numbers at the bottom of the stream, tonnage, waste ratio, energy per kilogram, and he did not believe them.
Then he took his lamp and raced into the tunnel.

The tunnel was beautiful. That was the thing he had not expected, and it undid him a little, walking through it. The walls were not rough-bored but *finished*, cut in long smooth strokes that overlapped like the grain of planed wood.

And at intervals along the floor, in neat staged rows, sat the ore. Processed. The machines had not just cut the corvite free; they had pulverized the waste rock and packed it into the walls, leaving a smooth finish. And the corvite itself they had crushed, graded, and pressed into dense dark bundles the size of bread loaves, wrapped in sheeting from their own supply spools and stacked with a regularity that no human crew on Dross had ever achieved or attempted.
